This is the second of two Summits this year, labeled 26.04 and 26.10 to mirror Ubuntu's release cycle. The timetable , hosted on the Discourse site, lists several talks on AI and agentic coding. events.excerpt: Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch. Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products . However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error. Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch. In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager. In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully. However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually. It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal. Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates
events.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install

events.excerpt: Hi all, If you work with more than one Cosmos chain, you’ve probably hit this: chain binaries don’t update themselves. After a network upgrade, the gaiad or osmosisd on your machine quietly goes stale, and you find out when a transaction fails or a query returns something odd. Cosmovisor solves this for running nodes, but nothing did for developers, CLI users and CI. I built cosmup to fill that gap. It’s a small Go CLI that reads the Cosmos chain registry, downloads the right binary for your platform, verifies its SHA256, and keeps versions side by side. $ cosmup check osmosis Local: v30.0.0 (/usr/local/bin/osmosisd) Network: v31.0.0 (via https://lcd.osmosis.zone) Status: does not match the network; run: cosmup install osmosis@v31.0.0 $ cosmup install osmosis Verified sha256 d435408b... Active: osmosis v31.0.0 What it does: install / use / list: install any version listed in the chain registry, switch between installed versions instantly check: compares your local binary with the version the live network runs, and shows scheduled upgrades (exits 1 on mismatch, so it works in CI) update: moves every installed chain to its recommended version cosmovisor: for validators, puts a verified upgrade binary into cosmovisor’s upgrades folder ahead of the upgrade height remove / prune: cleans up old versions testnets too (e.g. cosmoshubtestnet) Two design choices: Registry only. cosmup installs only chains and versions listed in cosmos/chain-registry, and only from the URLs listed there. Verified by default. If the registry has no checksum for a binary, cosmup refuses to install it un
events.title: Cosmup: install, switch and check Cosmos chain binaries (like nvm, for gaiad/osmosisd/...)

events.excerpt: arXiv:2606.00625v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reproducing software vulnerabilities is fundamental to security researchers, open-source maintainers, and educators. Yet, vulnerabilities are often hard to reproduce, and even when they can be reproduced once, recreating a software environment where the vulnerability can be exploited becomes harder and harder over time. We present NICE, the NIx CvE reproduction framework, which uses declarative recipes to build and automatically validate vulnerable environments. In NICE, a reproduced CVE comprises one or more NixOS virtual machine configurations, a scripted exploitation scenario, and machine-checkable assertions that provide factual evidence of exploitation. This design facilitates sharing, validation, review, and long-term reproducibility. Building on NICE, we construct a public archive of 56 reproduced vulnerabilities spanning multiple CWE categories, attack vectors, and target types (user-space, system software, kernel, and graphical applications), combining manually authored recipes with recipes produced by an LLM-based automated pipeline and merged after human review. We evaluate the feasibility of the automated pipeline on 110 real-world CVEs, achieving fully automated reproduction in 54.5% of the cases, at an average cost of $0.73 per CVE. The evaluation demonstrates that NICE provides a practical target for LLM-assisted recipe generation, while also identifying where human refinement or additional automation remains necessary.
events.title: NICE: A Framework for Declarative and Machine-Checkable Vulnerability Reproduction

This raises the question of how modular communication should be organised. events.excerpt: Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google. On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite. Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications. "An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains. The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others. events.excerpt: The Mozilla-backed Thunderbird project is getting closer to a wider launch of a hosted email service designed to complement its desktop mail app. Now known as Thundermail (what else?), the service was originally developed under the Thunderbird Pro banner, which encompassed paid email, appointment scheduling, and file-sharing services designed to generate additional revenue for the organization. The org has been inviting people from its Thundermail waitlist to try the service through an early-access program, and this writer just happened to be among them. Thundermail offers a web-based email interface and can also be accessed through the Thunderbird desktop app, the Thunderbird mobile app for Android, or other compatible email clients. The Thunderbird apps remain free. Users get an inbox with up to 15 email addresses and three custom domains, plus 30 GB of mail storage and 60 GB of send storage for Thunderbird Send, an end-to-end encrypted file-sharing and large-attachment service. That’s for starters – the org intends to offer those extra features and services at different price points. Yes, Thundermail is a paid service, which may put off some users who are used to free email accounts offered via Gmail, Outlook.com and Proton Mail, but with the first two of those you do get served ads along with your messages. The sign-up screens for Thundermail suggest the basic service will cost $6 per month, billed annually. This is roughly equivalent to the £55 we paid for a year on the early access program. We asked Thunderbird when we can expect to see Thundermail officially launched
events.title: Mozilla Thunderbird email service edges closer to launch with early access

events.excerpt: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices. Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash. "Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins. "About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs." Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare. Its latest report, " An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent ," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register , have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use. At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources

events.excerpt: Description Clean builds of sui-node are slow: about 164s in dev and about 296s in release on a 16-core Mac. This cuts them to about 130s in dev and about 231s in release without removing functionality. Each commit stands alone: Drop unneeded crates from the graph. sui-simulator re-exported Move package and build crates that nothing used. These pulled move-compiler and sui-sdk into the build. sui-indexer-alt-metrics now puts its postgres collector behind a postgres feature, so diesel and postgres are no longer built. No host build of sui-types for a build script. sui-package-management 's build.rs now reads the snapshot manifest JSON directly instead of depending on sui-framework-snapshot . Less code generation in sui-core . Spawn helpers box futures before tokio::spawn , so tokio compiles one task harness instead of one per future type. This costs one extra allocation per spawn. typed-store 's DBMap / SafeIter methods move the code that doesn't depend on the key and value types into non-generic functions. SuiNode::start_async returns a boxed future, so node startup compiles once in the sui-node library instead of again in the binary. rocksdb no longer waits for jemalloc. rocksdb's jemalloc feature only enables jemalloc's unprefixed malloc. The C++ define it adds isn't read by rocksdb's sources. typed-store now turns on that jemalloc feature directly, so rocksdb's C++ build script starts without waiting for jemalloc's. The resolved jemalloc features are the same as before. Test plan Covered by existing tests for the changed crates. Timings come from alternating clean cargo
